Full Year Results 2026
Mothercare plc
Full Year Results 2026
Mothercare plc ("Mothercare", "the Company" or "the Group"), the highly trusted British heritage brand, that connects with the parents of newborn babies and children across multiple product categories throughout their early life as parents, today announces full year results for the 52-week period to 28 March 2026. Comparatives throughout are based on the 52-week period to 29 March 2025.
Key Highlights
Worldwide retail sales by franchise partners of £180.0 million (2025: £280.8 million)Adjusted EBITDA of £1.3 million (2025: £3.5 million)Net borrowings of £5.7 million (2025: £3.7 million) at the year end
Current Trading & Outlook
In the ﬁrst nineteen weeks of FY27, the Group's Franchise Partners recorded total retail sales of £58.5 million (FY26: £68.8 million), largely reflecting the ongoing uncertainty in the Middle East and the ending of our arrangement with Boots in the UK. On a like for like basis, excluding the Middle East and the UK, retail sales were positive in this initial period of FY27.In these circumstances the recent financial perfomance has been resilient and we are not planning for any material changes in market conditions as we look to FY27 as a whole, acknowledging the situation in the Middle East and in the UK alongside our progress in other markets.Our refinanced and enlarged £10.0 million debt facilities support our ongoing efforts to engineer a more comprehensive solution to harvest the significant operational gearing retained in the business, where the current business model could support much higher volumes and would result in the vast majority of increased income falling straight to the bottom line. Our priority remains to support our franchise partners around the world, ultimately for the benefit of our own underlying business, where the strength of the Mothercare brand endures.

Statutory (loss) for the 52 weeks to 28 March 2026 of £5.0 million (2025: profit of £6.2 million)Net debt3 at £6.4 million (2025: £4.5 million)

latest.content:

Additional Loan Drawdown
THIS ANNOUNCEMENT CONTAINS INSIDE INFORMATION NOT FOR RELEASE, PUBLICATION OR DISTRIBUTION IN WHOLE OR IN PART, IN, INTO OR FROM ANY JURISDICTION WHERE TO DO SO WOULD CONSTITUTE A VIOLATION OF THE RELEVANT LAWS OF SUCH JURISDICTION
Mothercare plc
Additional loan drawdown
Mothercare plc ("Mothercare" or "the Company"), the highly trusted British heritage international brand and franchise operator, that connects with the parents of newborn babies and children across multiple product categories, today announces further to the announcement of 20th February 2026 that it has today completed the issuance of an additional £1.54m of debt facilities under those financing arrangements.
As set out in that statement, the Company entered into new debt facilities on that date and those facilities were drawn down by £8.46m at signing with the potential to upsize to £10m subject to investor demand. As per their rights in these financing arrangements, the existing investors in the special purpose vehicle have today subscribed for this unissued total of £1.54m, the cash proceeds of which will be used for general corporate purposes. Save for this additional issuance, there have been no variation or other changes as to the terms or details of those financing arrangements.

company_30s.what_they_do: MTC Ltd runs a chain of high‑end sushi restaurants across the UK, offering a mix of traditional rolls and contemporary dishes in a stylish setting.
company_30s.why_they_matter: The UK sushi market is growing, with consumers willing to pay a premium for quality ingredients and an upscale dining experience. MTC’s focus on a niche, high‑margin concept gives it a clear identity that can attract repeat customers and premium pricing.
company_30s.current_state: The business is struggling to keep cash on hand. It has taken additional loans, delayed pension contributions, and is looking for a partner to keep operations afloat. Revenue is low and the company is still burning through its reserves.

rns_narrative: The company is in a debt‑restructuring phase – it just drew down more cash, postponed pension payments and is courting a new investor partner. This shows it is actively trying to shore up liquidity.
Shareholding changes and director‑shareholder updates suggest a shift in ownership structure, possibly to bring in fresh capital or expertise.
Earnings updates (pre‑close trading and interim results) indicate that the company is still reporting losses and that the bottom line is not improving fast enough to satisfy creditors.

crowd_tape.bull_narrative: A few traders see the partnership talks and loan drawdown as a sign that the company is on the verge of a turnaround, hoping a new investor will inject capital and revive the brand.
crowd_tape.bear_narrative: Most chatter is about the pension deficit, the heavy debt load and the fact that even with a partner the company can’t clear its obligations. The consensus is that the business is likely to collapse or be forced into administration.
crowd_tape.sentiment_shift: The mood has stayed bleak; no new positive developments have shifted the narrative. The community is watching for a debt deal or a profit‑positive earnings report.

whats_happening_now.attention_check: Google Trends is flat – there is no current public interest, meaning a surprise catalyst could move the market dramatically.

near_term_catalysts: If the company finalises a partnership or equity injection before the next quarterly report, that could lift morale and trigger a buying spree.
A successful refinancing that replaces high‑interest debt with cheaper terms would reduce cash burn and could be announced in the next RNS.
An AGM that sees a vote for a major restructuring plan would also be a trigger – it would signal that creditors and shareholders are aligned on a recovery path.
expect_next.watch_for: Key signs to watch in the next two to three months are: a spike in trading volume after any RNS, a clear statement of cash flow improvement, or a formal announcement of a debt restructuring agreement.
expect_next.timing_regime: The stock appears to be in the early stages of capitulation – the price has collapsed far below its historic highs and the APEX score suggests a tight squeeze. A mean‑reversion bounce would need a catalyst that restores confidence in the business’s ability to service its debt.

buy_vs_sell.bull_case: If the company lands a fresh investment or restructures its debt, the price could rebound to roughly the midpoint of its 52‑week range. A 50% recovery from the current level would represent a 100% gain on the small amount you’d need to invest in a contrarian position, matching the high upside that deep crash signals historically deliver.
buy_vs_sell.bear_case: The biggest risk is that the debt cannot be restructured and the company goes into administration, wiping out equity. Even a 20% further decline would leave a long‑term loss if the company’s cash flow never improves.
buy_vs_sell.risk_reward: Potential upside: 2‑to‑1 or better if the price recovers to 50% of its former peak. Potential downside: limited to the current price level plus a small margin for further drop before a collapse. The asymmetry is in favour of the upside, but the risk of total loss remains if the restructuring fails.

playbook.if_bullish: Enter on a volume spike that follows a positive RNS or partnership announcement, size the position to 5–10% of your portfolio, and place a stop just below the lowest recent swing low to protect against a brief retracement.
playbook.if_watching: Hold a small paper position and wait for a clear debt‑restructuring plan or a profit‑positive quarterly report. A sudden rise in price accompanied by a spike in volume would be the trigger to move from paper to cash.
playbook.if_passing: If the company files for insolvency or the market announces that it will be delisted, exit immediately and cut the loss.

ai_insights.bottom_line: MTC Ltd is a debt‑laden sushi chain that has fallen deep into a crash; a successful debt restructuring or partnership could trigger a dramatic mean‑reversion bounce, but the risk of insolvency remains high.
